newsitem.title: JAPAN: Pressure builds on Japan's debt-ridden contractors.
newsitem.headline: Pressure builds on Japan's debt-ridden contractors.

text.p: A growing list of Japanese construction firms is devising drastic plans to deal with heavy debts, but analysts remain unimpressed and expect fears of a collapse at several contractors will continue to haunt the sector.
Fujita Corp, a medium-sized Japanese construction company, this week became the second publicly traded Japanese contractor in less than a week to announce a sweeping restructuring programme.

"The industry may have entered a long winter," said Toshihiko Okino, an analyst at Schroders Japan Ltd. "The hard times might continue for the next seven to eight years, like they did in the late 1970s to mid-1980s."

Medium-sized contractors are likely to be squeezed further, analysts said, by the government's targeted 10 percent cut in public works spending over the three years beginning with the next fiscal year, which starts in April 1998.

Moreover, Japanese banks, under pressure by new Finance Ministry rules to clean up their own balance sheets, may cut off new credit to construction firms they deem unlikely to overcome heavy debt burdens, allowing them to collapse.

A Fujita spokesman said that the contractor's three-year restructuring programme aims, by March 2000, to cut interest-bearing debt by 157.4 billion yen ($1.34 billion) to 480 billion yen ($4.10 billion) and to trim the workforce by nearly 10 percent to 4,900.
It also aims to boost profit margins on construction projects to 10.1 percent in 1999/2000 from 8.9 percent in 1996/97, he said.
He added that Fujita's main creditor bank, Sakura Bank Ltd, had said it would go along with the plan, and other banks were likely to follow suit.

Last Wednesday, the Mitsui industrial group, which includes Sakura Bank, pledged its full support to Mitsui Construction Co Ltd after the troubled contractor unveiled a three-year restructuring programme.
The seriousness of the construction sector's woes was highlighted in July, when two publicly listed general contractors, Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd and Tada Corp, collapsed under the weight of heavy debts.
Some analysts, however, were unimpressed by the restructuring plans at Mitsui and Fujita.

"The programmes were apparently intended to avert fears in the stock market and at local subcontractors about their creditworthiness," one analyst said. "But they did not include measures to solve problems at their troubled affiliates and did not take into account the likelihood of interest rate increases."
On Monday, Fujita's share price rose 17.8 percent to close at 106 yen, up from Friday's close at 90 yen and a record low of 79 yen hit during intraday trade on Friday.
Analysts said that only speculators would be interested in construction shares priced below 200 yen.
Several medium-sized general contractors have already been pushed below that level amid worries about potential debt-related difficulties.

Another probable source of pressure is the banks. They have yet to set aside loss reserves for potential problem loans to the construction sector, as many builders have managed to pay interest on their bank loans and to post yearly profits, both prerequisites to win public works contracts from local governments.
Japanese banks have a total of 31 trillion yen ($264 billion) in loans outstanding to the sector.

Many banks will soon be forced to let financially weak builders go under, however, when the Finance Ministry introduces stricter rules on assessing banks' bad assets, beginning with earnings reports for the fiscal year ending in March 1998.
"The future of Japan's construction companies will depend on how their creditor banks act," said Yoshinobu Yamada, a banking analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.
